idiom_name: explicit state machine (enum state + switch) with a function-pointer listener array
implementation_notes: C cannot carry the pattern's guarantee: there are no closures or generics, no sealed union of event and state types, no stream abstraction and no UI binding that replays a current state to new subscribers, so the typed event hierarchy and the observable state stream degrade into an enum tag plus a switch statement - the structure of the pattern without its payoff. What remains workable is an explicit state machine: one enum for states (enumerations give named constants scope and debugger visibility), one enum plus a tagged struct for events, a transition function mapping (state, event) to the next state, and a fixed-size array of function pointers as the listener registry. Keep UI coordination in the view layer (GTK signals, LVGL callbacks) and hand listeners a copied state value so nothing borrows out of the dispatch.
pitfalls: Function-pointer listeners carry no lifetime: every registration must be paired with an explicit removal, or the registry calls into freed modules.
A callback handed a pointer to the live state (or to a stack snapshot) dangles as soon as dispatch returns; pass a copied value and document the ownership rule.
There is no equality or conflation notion: re-dispatching the same event re-notifies every listener, and a listener that calls dispatch re-enters the switch recursively.
Cross-thread dispatch (worker plus GUI thread) needs a lock or a message pump; a bare switch over a shared enum is a data race.
alternative: Keep the screen's state in a hand-written state machine - enum state tag plus tagged event struct plus switch transition plus a small array of listener callbacks - and leave rendering and event capture to the view layer's framework (GTK/GTK4 signals, LVGL, or Qt when C++ is available); do not build typed event hierarchies or a replayable stream in C.
